newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW-CNS margins off on non-US sales.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-CNS margins off on non-US sales.

text.p: Gross profit margin has declined this year at CNS Inc because of increased international sales, but company president Richard Jahnke said domestic margins are sustainable at about 66 percent.
"As international becomes a larger part of our business mix, the margin will go down," Jahnke said in an interview with Reuters this week at a Dain Bosworth conference in Minneapolis.
Gross margin so far this year is at about 60 percent, compared with 66 percent at the end of 1995. "That's due to the international dilution," Jahnke said.

The company's blockbuster product -- the Breathe Right nasal strip -- is marketed outside the United States by Minnesota Mining & Manufacturing Co, which buys the product at a discount from CNS and ships it to 26 countries.
"The arrangement gives us the volume benefits of their business on our domestic cost structure," Jahnke said.
Sales at Minneapolis-based CNS were $48 million in 1995, up from $2.8 million in 1994 and $93,000 in 1993 -- a meteoric increase that still has Jahnke shaking his head in disbelief.
"Let's face it, any product eventually saturates its market," but he said Breathe Right is nowhere near that point.
"The estimates out on the Street put us at 35-40 percent sales growth in '97, and everbody's looking at 65-70 percent this year," Jahnke said.
"We can't keep up those percentages" indefinitely, he said, but added that Breathe Right has a long way to go.
Studies show about seven percent of U.S. households have tried Breathe Right -- an adhesive strip placed across the bridge of the nose to enlarge the nasal air passages.
Typically, cold and congestion remedies are tried by 50 percent of households. "Getting that level of penetration for first-time trial seems reasonable" for Breathe Right, he said.
Market research shows 30 percent of households that try Breathe Right buy it again, he said.
Production is running smoothly after some initial hiccups. An inventory shortage hit in the first quarter of 1995, when demand for Breathe Right suddenly jumped tenfold.
"Somebody asked me once, 'Well, why didn't you forecast that.' I had to say, well, if somebody had forecast that, we'd have had to fire them, once we stopped laughing," he said.
Shares in CNS were up 1 at 18-5/8 at 1400 EDT/1800 GMT Friday.
